summary: All three specialist inputs were available for this diagnostic run (financial_findings.json, data_quality_findings.json, contract_risk_findings.json) and every finding from each is reflected in the six action items below, ranked by combined annual dollar impact (roughly $1.09M-$2.56M in aggregate). The most valuable cross-agent correlation is between the financial-analyst's AR-days deterioration (41 to 71 days, ~$565K-$671K of cash tied up) and the data-quality auditor's CRM findings: 6 of 14 accounts are missing a working contact channel (phone/email/name) and 2-3 accounts carry stale or missing last-activity dates - the collections team may literally lack a working number for some of the accounts whose receivables are aging. A second correlation, run at lower priority but no less real, ties the financial-analyst's gross-margin-compression finding (COGS/revenue up ~1.7 points starting Dec-25, currency-neutral) to two contract-reviewer findings the financial analyst had no visibility into on its own: an uncapped, carrier-set monthly freight fuel surcharge, and a raw-materials contract that escalates prices every anniversary by a guaranteed 4%+ 'without further notice to or consent from' Acme. Three other financial-analyst findings (the EBITDA sign-flip, the likely OpEx currency-conversion artifact in the normalizer, and the source ledger's Gross Profit column disagreeing with computed Revenue-COGS) all concentrate in the identical Dec-25 through Feb-26 window and are treated as one financial-reporting-reliability action item rather than summed, since they are different views of the same underlying data problem and summing them would double-count. The remaining two items cover contract lock-in risk that limits Acme's ability to walk away from either vendor (raw-materials 85% volume commitment plus its auto-renewal window; freight's auto-renewal plus lack of any termination-for-convenience right), and general CRM hygiene (duplicate accounts, a blank-name record, missing revenue/activity fields, region-naming drift) not already captured in the collections item.

action_items.problem: Days sales in AR climbed from a 41.5-day average (Mar-Jun-25) to a 68.7-day average (Dec-25-Feb-26), tying up an estimated $565,000-$671,000 in cash with no reversal (financial_findings: 'Working capital deterioration: AR days climbed from 41 to 71 with no reversal'). This compounds with two data-quality findings the financial analyst could not see on its own: 6 of 14 CRM accounts (43%) are missing a core contact channel - phone, email, or contact name - needed to act on a collections or renewal signal, an estimated $24,000-$64,000/year of revenue exposure (data_quality_findings: 'Missing contact-channel fields ... block owner outreach'), and 2-3 accounts (A-1006, A-1010, A-1011) carry last-activity dates 2-3 years stale or missing entirely, an estimated $6,000-$14,000/year (data_quality_findings: 'Stale or missing last-activity dates risk silent account abandonment'). Together this points to a breakdown in the collections/account-management workflow, not just a demand-side issue: the accounts whose receivables are aging may be exactly the ones collections has no working number for.
action_items.solution: Stand up a weekly AR aging review with credit-hold triggers past 60 days, paired with a one-time CRM contact-data cleanup sprint: backfill/re-verify phone, email, and last-activity fields for the flagged accounts (A-1002, A-1003, A-1006, A-1007, A-1010, A-1011, A-1012, A-1014), and require at least one working contact channel plus a recent last-activity date before any account can be marked active in the CRM going forward.
action_items.tradeoffs: Requires dedicated ops/finance time upfront (est. 1-2 FTE-weeks for CRM cleanup plus ongoing collections analyst capacity); enforcing credit holds too aggressively could create friction or slow order fulfillment for legitimate slower-paying customers.
action_items.success_metrics: AR days back to a <=45-50 day baseline within 2 quarters; 100% of active accounts carry a working contact channel and a last-activity date within 90 days; zero accounts flagged 'stale >180 days' on the next quarterly CRM audit.

action_items.problem: Reported EBITDA swings from a +$40,972/month average (Mar-Nov-25) to -$33,634/month (Dec-25-Feb-26), an $850,000-$1,090,000 annualized swing on its face (financial_findings: 'As-reported EBITDA turns negative in Dec-25 through Feb-26'). But that raw number is unreliable: the normalizer's blanket USD-to-CAD conversion rule likely overstates Dec-Feb OpEx by ~$70,670/month, a $212,000-$848,000/year annualized effect (financial_findings: 'Likely normalizer artifact: blanket USD-to-CAD conversion probably overstates Dec-Feb OpEx'), and the source ledger's own Gross Profit column disagrees with computed Revenue-COGS by $60,000-$63,000/month in those same three months, with two additional months left as unevaluated formula strings (financial_findings: 'Source ledger's own Gross Profit column materially disagrees with Revenue-COGS'). All three findings concentrate in the identical Dec-25 through Feb-26 window, indicating one live data-reliability problem in the source finance file and normalization logic, not three unrelated ones - so the raw $850K-$1.09M EBITDA figure should not be used for planning until reconciled.
action_items.solution: Confirm directly with the controller what currency OpEx was actually recorded in for Dec-25/Jan-26/Feb-26, and which Gross Profit figure (stated or recomputed) actually reached the board, before using EBITDA for any decision; fix pipeline/normalize.py to check currency per line item rather than blanket-converting Revenue, COGS, and OpEx together whenever 'USD' appears in the Notes column; tighten spreadsheet controls on the source financials file so formulas are evaluated and Gross Profit is derived consistently from Revenue-COGS.
action_items.tradeoffs: Restating 3 months of financials may be uncomfortable if figures were already circulated to the board or a lender; fixing the normalizer requires re-validating prior periods too, which takes analyst time; added source-file controls create friction for whoever maintains the monthly ledger.
action_items.success_metrics: Reconciled Dec-Feb EBITDA and Gross Profit figures confirmed with the controller within 30 days; normalizer passes a per-line-item currency-check unit test; zero Gross-Profit-vs-computed discrepancies in the next 2 reporting cycles.

action_items.problem: Gross margin compressed ~1.7 points starting Dec-25 (COGS/revenue up from a 65.06% to a 66.75% average), a real, currency-neutral $125,000-$150,000/year hit (financial_findings: 'Gross margin compressed ~1.7 points starting Dec-25'). The contract-reviewer's findings, done independently, point to two plausible direct drivers landing in COGS/freight-in-COGS on the same timeline: the raw-materials supply agreement escalates Base Prices every anniversary by the greater of a guaranteed 4% or the trailing Statistics Canada IPPI change, 'without further notice to or consent from' Acme - ~12.5% cumulative over the 3-year term, $40,000-$200,000/year (contract_risk_findings: vendor_contract_raw_materials.pdf, pricing_escalator); and the freight contract carries an uncapped, carrier-set monthly fuel surcharge explicitly carved out of the 'rates remain fixed' protection, $15,000-$100,000/year (contract_risk_findings: vendor_contract_freight.pdf, pricing_escalator).
action_items.solution: Pull the actual Schedule A invoiced amounts for both vendors and reconcile them month-by-month against the COGS ratio inflection to quantify exactly how much of the 1.7-point compression is escalator/surcharge-driven versus other input-cost mix; open renegotiation with both vendors ahead of the next notice window (raw materials: 60 days pre-anniversary; freight: 120 days pre-renewal) to cap the escalator or surcharge, or begin a competitive re-tender in parallel.
action_items.tradeoffs: Triggering either notice window forces an all-or-nothing choice between accepting the next price increase and exiting the whole supply/freight relationship (see the related contract lock-in items below); re-tendering carries switching costs and short-term supply-continuity risk; the raw-materials supplier has no contractual obligation to negotiate given the 'without consent' language.
action_items.success_metrics: Gross margin back above 34.5% within 2 quarters; a signed amendment capping the raw-materials escalator or the freight fuel surcharge; a documented vendor-cost reconciliation showing the escalator/surcharge share of the COGS increase.

action_items.problem: The raw-materials contract's 85% minimum-requirements commitment blocks Acme from shifting volume to a cheaper supplier even after the escalator above raises prices (contract_risk_findings: vendor_contract_raw_materials.pdf, 'Volume-commitment lock-in', $30,000-$150,000), and the 60-day non-renewal notice sits inside the identical window as the price-increase notice - meaning avoiding one year's escalator means terminating the entire supply relationship with a supplier whose standard lead time is only 10 business days, leaving little runway to re-source (contract_risk_findings: vendor_contract_raw_materials.pdf, auto_renewal, $15,000-$80,000).
action_items.solution: Begin qualifying a second raw-materials supplier now, ahead of the next 60-day window, so Acme has a credible alternative in hand if it ever needs to exercise non-renewal; in parallel, negotiate the 85% requirement down (e.g., to 70-75%) at the next renewal so a limited share of volume can be shopped competitively without breaching the contract.
action_items.tradeoffs: Dual-sourcing raises procurement complexity and may forgo volume-discount pricing from the incumbent; qualifying a backup supplier has its own upfront cost and lead time.
action_items.success_metrics: A qualified backup raw-materials supplier on file within 6 months; a renegotiated requirements commitment below 85% at the next renewal; no missed non-renewal deadlines going forward, tracked via a contract calendar.

action_items.problem: The freight contract auto-renews for successive 24-month terms unless Acme gives 120 days' written notice, and a renewed term carries no right to renegotiate rates at all (contract_risk_findings: vendor_contract_freight.pdf, auto_renewal, $25,000-$150,000); separately, there is no termination-for-convenience right during the Initial Term or any Renewal Term (contract_risk_findings: vendor_contract_freight.pdf, termination, $10,000-$75,000). Together, a single missed 120-day deadline locks Acme into 24 more months of fixed base rates - while the fuel surcharge above keeps moving every month - with no contractual exit.
action_items.solution: Calendar the 120-day non-renewal deadline now, well ahead of the next Initial/Renewal Term expiration, and use it as leverage to negotiate a rate-renegotiation right into the next renewal, or run a competitive freight RFP in parallel so Acme can credibly walk if the carrier won't add flexibility.
action_items.tradeoffs: Switching freight carriers mid-relationship risks short-term service disruption; negotiating away the 'no renegotiation' clause may require Acme to concede something else, such as a volume commitment or a longer initial term.
action_items.success_metrics: Non-renewal deadline tracked in a contract calendar with 150+ days of buffer; the next renewal includes either a rate-renegotiation right or a capped/indexed fuel surcharge; a completed competitive freight RFP on file.

action_items.problem: Beyond the collections-linked CRM issues above, the CRM carries broader hygiene problems (data_quality_findings): 4 duplicate account pairs from inconsistent legal-suffix naming double-count revenue and rep effort (A-1001/A-1002, A-1004/A-1005, A-1009/A-1010, A-1013/A-1014, $12,000-$24,000); one fragmented record with a blank company name on an active $205,000 account (A-1007/A-1008, $3,000-$6,000); 2 accounts with no Annual Revenue on file (A-1003, A-1012) plus 1 with no Last Activity date, degrading forecasting ($8,000-$20,000); and 3 accounts where Region is spelled out in full instead of abbreviated (A-1002, A-1005, A-1014), silently excluding them from territory rollups ($3,000-$9,000).
action_items.solution: Run a one-time dedupe/merge pass on the 4 duplicate pairs and the fragmented A-1007/A-1008 record; enforce required fields at data-entry time (Company Name always populated, Region as an enforced picklist rather than free text, Annual Revenue required); backfill the 2 missing-revenue and 1 missing-activity records from source systems.
action_items.tradeoffs: Merging accounts risks losing distinct historical activity or notes if not done carefully; enforcing required fields at entry may slow rep data entry and needs rep buy-in and training.
action_items.success_metrics: Zero duplicate accounts and zero blank required fields on the next quarterly CRM audit; Region converted to an enforced picklist; territory revenue rollups reconcile to source revenue within 1%.
